claims.text: The investigated material is additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy.
The starting alloy has a single-phase FCC matrix.
The starting microstructure is uniform.
The starting material has minimal pre-existing oxide scale.
Elevated-temperature degradation is governed primarily by selective oxidation of Ti and Al.
Selective oxidation of Ti and Al forms a brittle, poorly adherent oxide scale.
Higher oxygen partial pressure produces more rapid oxide-scale growth and thickening.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between the oxide and the HEA causes the oxide scale to spall.
Oxide-scale spallation exposes fresh substrate and enables further oxidation.
Repeated oxidation and spallation lead to intergranular crack nucleation and propagation.
Crack propagation and coalescence eventually cause catastrophic failure.
Lower oxygen partial pressures produce a thinner, more coherent and adherent oxide scale.
A thinner, more adherent scale under lower oxygen activity delays degradation and failure.
Relative to the air baseline, high-oxygen exposures will produce thicker, less adherent scales.
Relative to the air baseline, high-oxygen exposures will produce more metal/oxide interfacial cracking and earlier mechanical degradation.
Reducing or low-oxygen atmospheres will produce minimal oxide growth and delayed degradation relative to the air baseline.
There is a transition threshold in oxide behavior as a function of oxygen partial pressure.
In ambient air at 700–800 °C for up to 100 hours, the alloy maintains a thin, stable oxide scale and relatively intact mechanical integrity.
The proposed governing behavior applies between 700 and 800 °C for exposure durations up to 100 hours.
Outside the stated temperature and duration limits, additional high-temperature mechanisms or kinetic changes may influence degradation.
